description: One of about seventeen substantially intact Lancasters worldwide. Acquired from the French Aeronavale on 1 December 1962 and painted in No. 463 Squadron markings as JO-D (D-Dog), an aircraft that completed 93 operations.
aliases: Lancaster; Lancaster B.VII; Lancaster BVII; JO-D

description: Acquired from England in 1959 as the RAAF Association WA's first aircraft and originally mounted on a pole outside its Perth headquarters; restored and moved into the north hangar in 1985.
aliases: Spitfire; Spitfire F.22; Spitfire F22; c/n CBAF.70

description: Full-scale replica acquired from New Zealand in August 1985 and displayed outside at the entrance, painted as TB592 of No. 451 Squadron RAAF; the museum notes the NI-V code letters are historically inaccurate for this serial. Some sources describe it as an LF.XIVe replica.
Painted in United States Navy colours; unveiled in the south hangar in 2010. The number carried is the identity as displayed.
Delivered to the RAAF in August 1945; displayed in RAAF colours carrying the name Flagship (ADF-Serials).
aliases: C47; C47B; Dakota; Skytrain; Flagship; c/n 34220

description: Built at Fishermens Bend in 1955 under licence. The rear fuselage is in fact from A84-248 and that aircraft carries A84-230's rear fuselage; the maintenance records do not record the swap (ADF-Serials).
aliases: Canberra; Canberra B.20; Canberra B20; Canberra Mk 20

description: Served with No. 1 Applied Flying Training School; approved for disposal 10/02/1970 and arrived at the RAAFA museum on 28 May 1970 (ADF-Serials).
aliases: Vampire; DH115; Vampire T.35A; Vampire T35A; c/n 4101

description: Entered RAAF service October 1940, civil registered VH-AHP in 1966 and withdrawn from use 1969; displayed in yellow RAAF markings (ADF-Serials).
aliases: DH82; DH82A; Tiger Moth; VH-AHP; c/n DHA162

description: Wirraway Mk III. Transferred to Midland Technical College in 1959 and airlifted by helicopter to Bull Creek on 20 July 1973. Restored in a silver RAAF scheme but painted in error as A20-668, in No. 5 Squadron code BF-R although it never served with that unit (ADF-Serials).

Ex-RAAF A3-31, sold in 1946 and registered to MacRobertson Miller Aviation; the personal aircraft of Horrie Miller. Displayed at the Horrie C Miller Museum in Broome until moved to Bull Creek in 2002. One of four surviving Wackett trainers (ADF-Serials).
Displayed painted as A7-025 in No. 25 Squadron markings; a wing from A7-009 was used in the restoration. First flight 31/10/1969, served with 2 FTS and No. 79 Squadron (ADF-Serials).
aliases: MB326; MB326H; Macchi; A7-025; CA-30; CA30

description: Ex-US Army 72-21597, delivered to the RAAF November 1973; served with 35 and 5 Squadrons then Army 171 Squadron and finally ARDU at RAAF Edinburgh, carrying dual Army and RAAF/ARDU titles. Delivered to the museum 29 July 2014 and displayed between the two hangars (ADF-Serials).

Crew module only. Allocated USAF serial 67-0140, first flight 24 December 1968, delivered to the RAAF 1 October 1973 and served with 1 and 6 Squadrons; the first locally modified F-111C to take Pave Tack in 1985. The airframe was scrapped in 2011 and the crew module delivered to the museum in May 2013 (ADF-Serials).

The first Australian Hornet, first flight 13/08/1984, delivered 09/03/1985 and ferried non-stop to Australia with A21-102. Served with No. 2 Operational Conversion Unit and ARDU; preserved at the museum from 12 April 2023 (ADF-Serials).
aliases: F/A18; FA18; FA18B; F/A18B; F/A-18B; Hornet; c/n 213

description: Ex-Royal Air Force; the fleet served on Operations Telic, Herrick and Shader before Tornado retirement in 2019. Donated by the RAF and transferred to the museum in 2022; the only Tornado displayed outside the United Kingdom.

Ex-Royal Canadian Air Force 23702, then South African Air Force 383, Kempton Park Technical College and a private owner at Lanseria before reaching New Zealand and Australia. Stored dismantled between the two museum hangars; museum staff have indicated restoration would be difficult.
Complete airframe displayed in the north hangar.
Cockpit section only, named The Islander.
Auster J/5 Adventurer light aircraft.
aliases: Auster J/5; Auster J5; Adventurer; c/n 2894

description: de Havilland Moth Minor light aircraft.
Percival Proctor Mk III.
aliases: P34; P34A; Proctor; Proctor III; c/n K392

description: Sud Aviation-built Gardan Horizon modified so visitors can work the controls. Painted to represent Robin Sugar Bird Lady Miller's aircraft although it is not the type she flew regularly; wears both Australian and French registrations.
aliases: GY80; GY80180; GY80-180; Horizon; F-OCLI; c/n 215

description: Full-scale replica painted in the markings of Bristol Tourer G-AUDK of Western Australian Airways; deliberately left unskinned on one side to show the internal structure.
Three-quarter scale non-flying replica built in the mid 1980s by Ansett engineer Frank Matthews of Maddington, Western Australia.
aliases: Sopwith Camel; Camel; F1; M6394 F

description: Full-scale replica built in 1984 by Ansett engineer Frank Matthews at the museum, using measurements and photographs taken from an earlier Demoiselle replica the museum once held.
Five-eighths scale Hawker Hurricane replica homebuilt, constructed, owned and flown by Arthur Winstanley; wears the code AF-W.

The second Flying Flea built by Bob Raper, who had built the first in Western Australia, an HM.14 tested at West Subiaco in 1936. Tandem-wing type; the tail marking reads HM.290 although the aircraft is a modified HM.293.
Heath Parasol homebuilt; a further rebuild of the airframe was under way in 2010.
Tailless glider, one of three Flying Planks known to survive in Australia; scratch-built and donated by Mr C K Gentle.
Homebuilt kit aircraft rebuilt at the museum from 2004 and dedicated to Daniel Florusse, a member of the museum's youth club; some parts including the nosewheel are non-original.
Kingfisher III glider built in 1960; owned for many years by the Clare Soaring Club, later the Balaklava Gliding Club, then the Gliding Club of Western Australia.
Imported into Australia in 1939 for the University of Sydney Soaring Club; the first high-performance glider brought to Australia and the first to fly more than 100 miles.
The world's first commercially available ultralight, designed in Australia by Ron Wheeler in the early 1970s.
Gyrocopter built in 1980 from a kit by Mr J Hahir, a farmer from Perillup, Western Australia, later owned by Jim and Lynette Herbert of Tambellup.
Gyrocopter built by Challenge in Western Australia with long-range fuel tanks and operated in the Pilbara; donated by Dr Noel Plumley in 2006.
Homebuilt helicopter constructed in 1978 by Robert L Wiggs; the tail is painted Scorpion 133 although the cockpit manufacturer's plate identifies it as a Scorpion II.
Built 1985, ex N8559D, registered VH-NDT April 1985 and cancelled in 2009 after a crash. Tailboom and rotors shortened; used as a travelling exhibit when not at the museum.
Built 2001 and cancelled from the register in 2010 after an accident. The tailboom is displayed in the southern hangar and the fuselage stored between the two hangars.
Genuine launcher carrying a replica Terrier-Sandhawk sounding rocket.
